items.title: Rivals in Israel Election Strike Tone of Triumph, but Outcome Is Far From Clear
items.summary: Addressing supporters after midnight, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Gadi Eisenkot, who leads a bloc of opposition parties, both expressed confidence that they will lead Israel’s next government. Vote counting could take days.
items.full_text: Several people whose relatives were killed or taken hostage in the Hamas-led attack on Israel on Oct. 7, 2023, are running for office in Tuesday’s election, the first national vote since the assault, which shook the country’s foundations and ignited its longest war. The exit polls, if accurate, suggest that neither Mr. Netanyahu’s bloc nor the one led by Mr. Eisenkot , a former military chief whose son was killed in the Gaza war, will be able to form a government without relying on two Arab parties that were projected to win as many as 17 or 18 seats in Parliament. Mr. Netanyahu effectively ruled out including them in a governing coalition, and Mr. Eisenkot and his partners have balked at the idea, too. One option analysts are already weighing is whether Mr. Netanyahu, who has led the most far-right government in Israeli history, could join with Mr. Eisenkot or others in the opposition to form a unity government. But a unity government would face major obstacles, given how deeply Mr. Eisenkot’s voters despise Mr. Netanyahu, and because the two would have to agree on which of them would serve as prime minister. Mr. Netanyahu is unlikely to give up control, while Mr. Eisenkot has called the prime minister unfit to lead Israel. Much remained unclear early Wednesday morning in Israel. Making matters even murkier, Israel’s exit polls have a spotty history of accuracy, particularly in tight races. Mr. Eisenkot appeared onstage past midnight at his post-election party and attempted to strike a tone of triumph — as well as defiance toward Mr. Netanyahu. “Tonight we got the answer: The public wants change,” he said. Mr. Netanyahu addressed his supporters a few hours later, invoking his relationship with President Trump and repeating his pre-election talking points about removing the threat of Iran. He sounded triumphant, saying it was clear that Likud had emerged as the largest party in Israel and mocking months of pre-election polls that showed his party trailing behind that of Mr. Eisenkot. “We must form a strong right-wing government,” he declared. In the coming days, after official vote totals are released and parliamentary seats are allocated to parties, Israel’s president, Isaac Herzog, will invite the party leader he thinks has the best chance to assemble a governing coalition. Such a coalition would usually have to be made up of at least 61 lawmakers, though Mr. Eisenkot has floated the idea of forming a minority government. One factor not reflected in exit polls are the hundreds of thousands of votes cast by Israelis at special polling stations, including at military bases, hospitals, prisons and embassies. In the previous election, those votes tended to favor the coalition of Mr. Netanyahu and his allies. Here’s what else to know: Arab parties: The exit polls pointed to at least one surprise in projecting that two Arab parties would win as many as 17 or 18 seats in the 120-seat Parliament. That would be their strongest showing ever, and potentially give them an important role in forming the next government. Read more › War fears: Amid reports that Mr. Netanyahu has been pushing for renewed attacks on Iran, Mr. Eisenkot warned him in his speech to supporters not to abuse his power as caretaker prime minister to influence the process of forming a new government. “Netanyahu, don’t dare use Israel’s security for your political needs,” he said. Mansour Abbas, the leader of Raam, told a television interviewer that the turnout showed that Arab voters, who make up about 20 percent of Israel’s population, had channeled their “frustration and despair” into “hope.” He said he wanted to replace Mr. Netanyahu’s government “in every possible way” and that his first priority was to “ensure that there is a chance of forming a government” that achieved that goal. The Arab parties’ strong showing may make them kingmakers. But building a governing coalition with Arab participation remains a fraught exercise in Israel. Many Israeli Jews believe that a parliamentary majority should not rely on the support of Arab lawmakers. People waiting to cast ballots in Umm al-Fahm, one of the largest Arab towns in Israel, on Tuesday. Credit... Ahmad Gharabli/Agence France-Presse — Getty Images Most Arab citizens are the descendants of Palestinians who remained in their homes during the 1948 Arab-Israel war at the time of Israel’s independence. Today, they mostly live in separate towns from Jewish Israelis and face violence and discriminatory housing policies. Over the decades, disagreements, including over Israel’s nature as a Jewish state, have led many Arab voters to avoid the ballot box. This week, many Arab voters said they were furious at Mr. Netanyahu for his treatment of the Palestinians in the West Bank and Gaza and for policies that they feel treat Palestinians in Israel as second-class citizens. Indeed, throughout the campaign, Mr. Netanyahu made overt appeals to anti-Arab prejudice. Of the two Arab parties that did well on Tuesday, only Raam has joined a coalition government in the past. That happened in 2021, when it joined the short-lived anti-Netanyahu coalition of Prime Minister Naftali Bennett. Raam’s participation in that government outraged many right-wing Jewish voters, and when it collapsed after roughly one year, they backed Mr. Netanyahu, who went on to form the most hard-line government in Israel’s history. That government now faces the possibility that it may be brought down by an election result that has been deeply shaped by robust Arab turnout. The longevity of his most recent governing coalition followed three years during which a cycle of collapsed coalitions and five snap elections had left the country without a functional government or national budget. In 2021, Israelis ousted Mr. Netanyahu from power and then returned him to office 18 months later. He had staged a previous comeback, in 2009, becoming prime minister a decade after his party was voted out of power. March 2021 Ousted by a single-seat majority In 2021, Mr. Netanyahu’s government collapsed after failing to pass a budget, setting off legislative elections. At the time, he had been indicted on charges of fraud, bribery and breach of trust , and the coalition he was leading was shaky. According to analysts , heading into an election was a gambit by Mr. Netanyahu to strengthen his grip on power before his criminal trial. But the electorate that voted that March didn’t give him the seats he needed, ending a period of 12 straight years in office for him. It took months of wrangling for an eclectic coalition of anti-Netanyahu forces to cobble together a single-seat majority in the Parliament. Naftali Bennett, a right-wing former ally of Mr. Netanyahu’s, led the coalition as prime minister, hammering out a deal with Yair Lapid, a centrist and former broadcaster who was appointed foreign minister. The eight-party coalition proved too unwieldy to endure. After two right-wing lawmakers defected and several on the left rebelled in critical votes, that government collapsed in June 2022 . November 2022 Returned to office by a hard-line coalition After the resulting elections, held in November 2022, Mr. Netanyahu returned to power as right-wing voters moved to more extreme parties, diminishing the center left. Mr. Netanyahu’s Likud party allied with far-right and ultra-Orthodox lawmakers to secure a clear majority in the Parliament , forming the most hard-line and religious conservative government in Israel’s history. The coalition accounted for 48.4 percent of the vote but had a parliamentary majority because two anti-Netanyahu parties — one leftist, one Arab nationalist — fell just short of the share of votes needed to obtain seats. It was a reminder of how tiny swings among voters can have a big effect under Israel’s parliamentary system. Mr. Netanyahu has since overseen an acceleration of the country’s rightward shift, including an effort to overhaul the judiciary that prompted huge street protests. Questions about whether his government could have better pre-empted the Oct. 7 attack have also become hot-button issues . In April, Mr. Lapid and Mr. Bennett said they would reconstitute their centrist alliance of 2021 for the 2026 election. Mr. Netanyahu will also face Gadi Eisenkot, a former military chief of staff who leads the largest opposition party . “It’s over,” he said. “It’s only a matter of time.” The comments were a reflection of Israel’s deepening global isolation, with even once-staunch allies imposing or threatening economic sanctions and embargoes after years of war in Gaza and rampant violence by Jewish settlers against Palestinians in the occupied West Bank. With settlers advancing into areas that were previously off limits, Britain last month decried what it called “ethnic cleansing” and announced trade sanctions on settlements that it said would also apply to entities that financed their construction. Though Israel’s banking system has not been directly targeted by sanctions, a dozen countries, including Canada, France and Spain, have said they support restrictions on trade with settlements, raising the prospect of further penalties that could affect Israeli financial institutions. Opponents of Mr. Netanyahu’s government decried his pronouncements, which also drew a rebuke from the generally reserved central bank. “Crypto currencies cannot serve as a route to bypass sanctions against Israel,” the Bank of Israel said in a statement. The bank added that the government would do better “to focus on preventing sanctions” and preserving Israel’s economic ties with its main trading partners. Commentators said that Mr. Netanyahu’s outlook sounded apocalyptic, and some said it was part of a scare campaign to improve his election prospects. items.title: Why Is Halloween Candy So Expensive?
items.summary: The average cost of a 100-piece bag has jumped 71 percent in the last five years. Consumers are thinking twice about what they’ll spend.
items.full_text:
Title: Why Is Halloween Candy So Expensive? - The New York Times

URL Source: https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/27/dining/halloween-candy-prices.html

Published Time: Wed, 28 Oct 2026 07:12:28 GMT

Markdown Content:
The economy has come for Tami Adolphson’s Halloween candy bowl.

Prices are so high this year that she considered turning off the porch light at her home near Salt Lake City and ignoring the doorbell. Ms. Adolphson, 63, and her husband, Lee, 68, closed down their trucking company and retired last year. The household budget is tight.

“We’re finding it harder to justify big prices even for the extremely satisfying ritual of handing out candy to kids,” she said. “We are not going to dip into savings for Halloween candy.”

But she couldn’t stand missing out. “I just can’t turn off the lights on these children,” she said. So last week she went to Costco and spent $21.39 on a bag of 90 mixed chocolate bars.

“We just won’t eat out one time this month,” she said. “It’s worth it to keep the tradition.”

Image

![Image 1: Tami Adolphson sits on concrete steps in front of a white house, looking forward with a slight smile. The porch is decorated with an orange pumpkin, a "Trick or Treat" sign and two skeletons on yellow chairs.](https://static01.nyt.com/images/2026/10/28/multimedia/28FD-halloween-candy2-tzgc/27FD-halloween-candy2-tzgc-articleLarge.jpg?quality=75&auto=avif&disable=upscale)

Ms. Adolphson was shocked at the price of a mixed bag of Halloween candy. Credit...Lindsay D'Addato for The New York Times

Anyone who has been to the grocery store recently has noticed higher prices. The cost of vegetables has jumped by 6 percent since last year. Beef is up by about 9 percent. But the price of Halloween candy — particularly chocolate — is even scarier.

One [recent analysis](https://groundworkcollaborative.org/work/halloween-candy-prices/) of the prices on 17 popular Halloween candy varieties showed a 15 percent jump from last year. The average price of a 100-piece bag is $16.96, up a staggering 71 percent since 2021, [according to FinanceBuzz](https://financebuzz.com/halloween-candy-inflation-study), a digital media company. Google searches for “cheap Halloween candy bulk” and “where to buy cheap Halloween candy” are up more than 5,000 percent year-over-year, said Megan Stoner, a spokeswoman for the company.

“The prices have gotten completely out of hand,” said Renni Turpin, 30. This is her first Halloween in a new neighborhood in Charlotte, N.C., and she wants to make a good impression. “No one wants to be the ‘raisin house,’” she said.

She would like to be the king-size candy bar house, but she works at a school and recently purchased her home. Even buying slightly less expensive candy, she figures she’ll spend about $100, or what she might spend on a week’s worth of groceries.

“It means that the Halloween tradition is now a financial burden,” she said. We asked New York Times readers if the price of candy was changing how they would approach trick-or-treating this year. More than 200 people responded, and almost 90 percent of them said they were adjusting their approach because the price of candy was so high. They are buying less, shopping sales and heading to bargain grocery outlets. Candy bowls are being cut with small bags of salty snacks, temporary tattoos, Play-Doh and low-cost trinkets they can buy in bulk.

Image

Renni Turpin, who is celebrating her first Halloween in a new neighborhood, wants to make a good impression. But cost will limit what she hands out. Credit...Swikar Patel for The New York Times

And then there is the classic method for stretching a small candy budget: Limit how many pieces a child (or rowdy teenager) can take.

Already, Halloween candy sales for the month ending Oct. 17 are down 6 percent compared with the same period last year, [according to NielsenIQ,](https://apnews.com/article/halloween-candy-sales-chocolate-prices-treats-0b1126f30969a21710ba995416c5b905) a market research firm.

Some people are abandoning the classic chocolate offerings. A [climate-driven global cacao supply crisis](https://www.nytimes.com/2025/10/30/climate/candy-chocolate-cocoa-prices-climate-change.html) sent prices to record highs in 2025, and companies began formulating their chocolate with [less expensive ingredients](https://www.grubstreet.com/article/chocolate-hersheys-reeses-conspiracy.html) and selling smaller packages of candy for more money. A bag of Reese’s miniatures that weighed 17.6 ounces last year weighs 15.8 ounces now and costs $1.50 more, according to analysts at the web research company Apify.

Luckily, Sour Patch Kids, Skittles and Nerd Gummy Clusters are less expensive and climbing in popularity among younger generations, who are turning away from chocolate in favor of candies with texture and sour or tangy flavors, said [Sally Lyon Wyatt](https://influentialwomen.com/connect/sallylyons-wyatt), an executive vice president for consumer goods and food service insights at Mintel, the market research firm.

“People will celebrate Halloween, but they’re going to use different tactics to do it,” she said. “Candy might be part of it, but maybe not as much as it had been in the past. There’s just going to be a bit more creativity.”

Image

Chocolate candy has gotten more expensive in the past few years, so more households are turning to sour, fruity and gummy candy.Credit...Swikar Patel for The New York Times

Cynthia Thomasset, who lives in Shillington, Pa., will likely supplement her candy stash with school supplies and stickers. She plans to have plenty on hand because her suburban neighborhood draws children from a nearby area that is one of the poorest in Pennsylvania.

But there will be no leftovers. “Usually I panic and go buy more right before,” she said, “but this year I am going to give out what I have and that’s it.”

Some households are getting even more creative. “I’ve switched to passing out ramen,” said Angie Vasey, a teacher who lives in Round Lake, Ill. The packets of instant soup were on sale this year for 10 cents apiece.

Magen Pillar, a communications director for United Way, is buying a $25 bag of candy and supplementing the holiday by building a bonfire and handing out bowls of her husband, Matt’s, homemade beef and bean chili from the driveway of their home in Columbus, Ind. It’s an inexpensive way to build a little neighborhood esprit de corps.

“It is hard to believe that a pot of chili is cheaper than a bag of candy,” she said.

Traditionalists remain, including those dedicated to making Halloween as special as they can with the ultimate prize: full-size candy bars.

Mitch Collins, 71, bought a mix of 270 Snickers, KitKats and other chocolate and packages of Skittles and Starbursts to hand out in his neighborhood in Oakdale, Calif.

“As a child, one time I received a full-size bar on Halloween,” he said. “I remember it to this day and want to share that joy with the kids that come to our home.”

He shelled out $269 at Costco.

“Yeah, it costs a lot,” he said, “but their joy is worth it.”
